questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they actually happen when you create customer_ltv.sql, stage it, and commit it for the first time, per Lessons 1 and 3.
items: The file sits in the working directory and git status reports it as an untracked file
git add customer_ltv.sql moves the change into the staging area
git status now shows the file under "Changes to be committed"
git commit -m "Add customer_ltv model" creates a permanent, timestamped snapshot in the repository
git log --oneline shows the new commit with its short hash and message
questions.explain: Every change moves through the same three stages: untracked in the working directory, staged once you deliberately git add it, then permanently recorded once you git commit it — with git log afterward confirming it actually landed.

questions.prompt: A folder already has three real .sql files in it, with no version control. After running git init inside it, what actually happens to those three files?
options: Nothing about the files changes — git init only creates a hidden .git folder alongside them; they aren't tracked yet
All three files are immediately staged and committed automatically
The files are moved into the new .git folder
git init refuses to run because the folder already contains files
questions.explain: git init creates a hidden .git folder inside the current directory — that's the entire repository. Nothing about the actual .sql files changes; running git status right after shows Git sees them but isn't tracking them yet, which is exactly correct and exactly what git add fixes.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: running git config ________ user.name "Jordan Lee" sets that name for every repository on the machine, not just the current project.
questions.explain: --global applies a git config setting to every repository on your machine. Without it, a setting only applies to the one repository you're currently in.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about branches, per Lesson 4.
options: git switch -c creates a new branch and switches to it in one step
Committing on a feature branch immediately changes what main looks like on disk for everyone
Switching back to main with git switch main changes your working directory's files to match main's last commit
git branch with no arguments lists every branch and marks the current one with an asterisk
A branch can only be created from main, never from another branch
questions.explain: git switch -c creates and checks out a branch in one step. Switching branches literally changes the files on disk to match that branch's last commit — a feature branch's commits don't touch main until a deliberate merge or rebase brings them together. git branch lists every branch with an asterisk on the current one. Nothing restricts branching to only ever starting from main.

questions.code:
git switch main
git merge rework-ltv-grain
questions.prompt: After running these two commands, how many parent commits does the resulting merge commit have, and which commits are they?
options: Two parents — the tip of main and the tip of rework-ltv-grain, with both histories preserved exactly as they happened
One parent — only the tip of rework-ltv-grain, since merging discards main's prior history
Zero parents — a merge commit starts a brand-new, independent history
Three parents — main's tip, the branch's tip, and the common ancestor they both started from
questions.explain: A merge commit has exactly two parents: the tip of the branch you merged into (main) and the tip of the branch you merged in (rework-ltv-grain). Neither branch's original history is rewritten — both lines of work are preserved side by side, joined at that one commit.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Lessons 4-6 to what it actually is.
right: Marks the start of your current branch's version inside a conflicted file
Joins two branches with a new commit that has two parents, preserving both histories exactly
Happens when two branches changed the same lines of the same file in different ways
Replays a branch's commits on top of another branch's current tip, producing new commits and a linear history
questions.explain: git rebase replays commits onto a new tip, producing a linear history with new commit hashes. git merge joins two branches with a two-parent commit, preserving both histories as-is. A conflict happens only when the same lines of the same file were changed differently by both sides. <<<<<<< HEAD marks where your current branch's version starts inside the conflicted file.

questions.code:
SELECT customer_id, churn_date
FROM subscriptions
<<<<<<< HEAD
WHERE status = 'cancelled'
=======
WHERE status IN ('cancelled', 'expired')
>>>>>>> feature/track-expired-subs
questions.prompt: churn_flags.sql still contains the block above. What does git status report right now, and what happens if you try to git commit without editing the file first?
options: git status reports churn_flags.sql as having an unresolved conflict, and Git won't let a normal commit complete until the marker lines are gone
git status reports the file as clean, since Git already merged both versions automatically
Git automatically deletes the losing version and commits the file as-is
git commit succeeds normally, permanently embedding the conflict markers into the file's history
questions.explain: Git writes both conflicting versions into the file along with the marker lines, but it won't guess which one you want. git status keeps flagging the file as unresolved, and committing is blocked, until every <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> line — along with whichever version you're discarding — is actually removed.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what git fetch does, as distinct from git pull?
options: git fetch downloads new commits from the remote and stores them locally without touching your working files or merging anything in; git pull does that same fetch and then immediately merges the new commits into your current branch
git fetch merges new remote commits into your current branch immediately; git pull only downloads them without merging
git fetch and git pull are two names for the exact same operation, with no functional difference
git fetch uploads your local commits to the remote; git pull downloads them
git fetch only works on the main branch; git pull works on any branch
git fetch requires a remote named origin specifically, while git pull works with any remote name
questions.explain: git fetch downloads whatever new commits exist on the remote and stores them locally, without touching your current working files — you can inspect what changed before deciding what to do. git pull is exactly git fetch followed immediately by git merge, run back to back as one command.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two commands' actual behavior — it's git pull that fetches and merges in one step, while git fetch alone deliberately stops short of touching your working files. That's exactly why git fetch is useful for inspecting a teammate's changes before they touch anything of yours.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: by convention, the first remote you connect a local repository to is named ________, though Git itself treats this as just a label, not a special keyword.
questions.explain: origin is purely a naming convention — Git would be equally happy if it were called github or upstream. What matters is that a URL is on file so push and pull know where to go.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why pull requests are worth opening even when you're the only person working on a project, per Lesson 9.
options: A pull request is a checkpoint — anything wired into CI runs automatically on it before the change ever reaches main
A pull request's description, diff, and comments stay attached to that change permanently, searchable later
Opening a pull request is required by Git itself before any merge can happen
Merging directly with git merge runs the exact same CI checks a pull request would
GitHub offers a "Compare & pull request" shortcut right after you push a new branch
questions.explain: A PR is both a checkpoint — CI runs against it before main is touched — and a permanent, searchable record of what changed and why. Pull requests are a GitHub convention, not something Git itself requires, and a plain git merge skips CI entirely since nothing triggers it.

questions.prompt: A reviewer leaves two line comments pointing out real problems in a dbt model's SQL and wants the merge button to stay blocked until they're fixed. Which review verdict actually accomplishes that?
options: Request changes
Comment
Approve
Closing the pull request without submitting a review
questions.explain: Request changes is the one verdict that blocks the merge button until the issues are resolved or dismissed. Comment is feedback with no verdict attached — it doesn't block anything — and Approve is what unblocks a merge, the opposite of what's needed here.

questions.prompt: Match each GitHub term from Lesson 11 to what it actually is.
right: A deadline or release grouping issues toward a shared target
A column-based view arranging issues and pull requests by status
A tracked unit of work that may or may not turn into a pull request
A tag used to filter and categorize issues at a glance
questions.explain: An issue tracks a unit of work before there's necessarily a diff for it. A label tags issues so they can be filtered at a glance. A project board arranges issues and PRs into status columns. A milestone groups issues toward a shared deadline or release.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order they happen when you push a new branch and get it merged through a real pull request, per Lessons 8-10.
items: git push -u origin <branch> sends the new branch's commits to GitHub for the first time
GitHub shows a "Compare & pull request" banner on the repository page
You open the pull request, choosing main as the base and your branch as the compare side
A reviewer leaves line comments and a suggestion, then submits a review
The reviewer picks Approve, unblocking the merge button
questions.explain: Pushing a new branch with -u is what first makes GitHub aware of it and offer the shortcut banner. Opening the PR sets the base and compare branches, after which a reviewer can comment, suggest, and finally submit the verdict that actually unblocks merging.

questions.prompt: This .gitignore is added to a repository where .env was already committed three commits ago. After adding this file and committing it, does .env stop showing up in git status, and does it disappear from the repository's history?
options: .env keeps showing as tracked and still exists in history — .gitignore only affects files Git doesn't already track, so it needs git rm --cached plus a credential rotation to actually fix
.env immediately stops being tracked and is scrubbed from every earlier commit automatically
.env stops showing in git status, but a teammate who already cloned the repo will still see it as tracked
Adding .gitignore causes Git to raise an error until the already-tracked file is manually deleted from disk
questions.explain: .gitignore only affects files Git doesn't already track. A file already committed needs an explicit git rm --cached to stop tracking it, and even then it's still recoverable from the repository's history — a leaked real credential needs rotating, not just untracking.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why a plain git diff on two Jupyter notebooks is often unreadable, per Lesson 13.
options: A .ipynb file is JSON containing cell code, markdown, metadata, and base64-encoded image output all in one structured file
This happens because of a bug in Jupyter that nbdime exists to patch around
nbdime parses the notebook's actual structure so it can show a code diff as a code diff and render a changed plot as an image comparison
Clearing a notebook's outputs before committing can reduce diff noise, at the cost of losing the saved output
Stale execution counts from out-of-order cell runs have no effect on how noisy a notebook's diff looks
questions.explain: A notebook is JSON — cells, metadata, and embedded base64 image output all in one file — which is the direct cause of unreadable diffs, not a bug. nbdime fixes this by parsing that structure itself. Clearing outputs and avoiding stale execution counts both genuinely reduce diff noise.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: running git lfs ________ "*.parquet" writes that pattern into .gitattributes, so any matching file is automatically stored as a pointer from then on.
questions.explain: git lfs track writes a pattern into .gitattributes. From that point on, any file matching the pattern is handled as an LFS pointer automatically on every future add and commit.

questions.prompt: Match each path in a dbt project's file tree to whether — and why — it belongs in Git, per Lesson 15.
right: Belongs in Git — hand-written transformation logic, no different from any other code
Never belongs in Git — regenerated every dbt run, committing it just creates pointless merge conflicts
Never belongs in Git — regenerated by dbt deps, not something anyone hand-edits
Never belongs in Git — contains credentials that would otherwise live permanently in history
questions.explain: models/ holds hand-written source and always belongs in Git. target/ and dbt_packages/ are both regenerated automatically and shouldn't be committed. .env holds credentials and belongs only in .gitignore.

questions.prompt: This is the entire content Git shows for a 129MB model artifact that's tracked with Git LFS. Why is the committed content this small instead of 129MB?
options: Git only ever tracks a small pointer file (version, hash, size) for an LFS-tracked path — the real content lives on a separate LFS server and is fetched on demand
Git compressed the 129MB file down to this size automatically, the same way it compresses any other committed file
This is a corrupted commit, and the real 129MB file was lost
LFS deleted the original file from disk once it was committed
questions.explain: Git LFS substitutes a tiny pointer file — a version tag, a hash, and a size — for the real content. Git's history stays small regardless of the actual file's size because it's the pointer being diffed and stored, not the file itself.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes Continuous Delivery from Continuous Deployment?
options: In Continuous Delivery, every change that passes CI is automatically packaged and release-ready, but a human still approves the actual release; in Continuous Deployment, every change that passes CI ships automatically with no human approval step
In Continuous Deployment, every change that passes CI is packaged but a human approves the release; in Continuous Delivery, changes ship automatically with no approval
Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment are two names for the identical practice
Continuous Delivery means testing happens manually; Continuous Deployment means testing happens automatically
Continuous Deployment only applies to application code, never to a dbt project's models
Continuous Delivery means merging code frequently; Continuous Deployment means merging it rarely
questions.explain: Continuous Delivery stops at release-ready with a human clicking the button to actually ship. Continuous Deployment removes that approval step entirely — every passing change ships automatically. Nothing about either practice is specific to application code; a dbt project's build/test/release steps fit the same shape.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes the exact same two practices but swaps which one has the human approval step. It's Continuous Delivery that keeps a human gate before release, and Continuous Deployment that ships automatically with none — getting the two backwards is exactly the mistake this lesson calls out as the most common one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in GitHub Actions' vocabulary, the disposable machine that actually executes a job's steps — for example ubuntu-latest — is called a ________.
questions.explain: The runner is the actual machine a job's steps execute on. An event triggers the workflow, a job is a set of steps run together, and each of those steps runs on a runner.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about required status checks, per Lesson 19.
options: A status check existing on a commit is not the same as it actually blocking a merge
Required status checks are configured on a branch protection rule, not inside the workflow YAML file itself
Once a workflow is added, GitHub blocks merging on a failing check automatically, with no extra configuration
A pull request's Checks tab rolls up every check across every commit on that PR into one place
Required status checks only apply to workflows triggered by a schedule, never by a pull request
questions.explain: A red X by itself is just a visual — the merge button stays clickable until a branch protection rule marks that specific check as required. That setting lives in repository Settings, not in the workflow file. The Checks tab rolls up results across every commit on the PR regardless of what triggered the workflow.

questions.code:
name: dbt CI
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install dbt-snowflake
      - run: dbt build
      - run: dbt test
questions.prompt: A teammate claims this workflow would still run even on a direct push to main with no pull request involved. Are they correct?
options: No — the on: block only lists pull_request targeting main, so a direct push triggers nothing here; a push trigger would have to be added separately
Yes — runs-on: ubuntu-latest makes this workflow run on every event type by default
Yes — any workflow in .github/workflows/ runs on every push and pull request automatically, regardless of what on: specifies
No — this workflow never runs at all, because listing dbt build and dbt test as two separate steps is invalid syntax
questions.explain: The on: block is what actually controls which events trigger a workflow — here it's scoped to pull_request against main only. A direct push to main matches a different event entirely and wouldn't trigger this specific workflow unless a push: trigger were added alongside it.

questions.prompt: Put these events in order, from a developer pushing a commit to a required status check actually blocking a merge button.
items: A commit is pushed to a branch with an open pull request
GitHub triggers the workflow because the push matches its on: conditions
The job runs its steps and finishes with a pass or fail exit code
That pass/fail result attaches to the commit as a status check, visible on the PR's Checks tab
Because the check is marked required under branch protection, a failing result keeps the merge button blocked
questions.explain: A push first has to match the workflow's trigger before anything runs. The job's steps then produce a pass/fail exit code, which attaches to that exact commit as a status check. Only because branch protection marks that check as required does a failing result actually block the merge button, rather than just showing a red X for show.

questions.code:
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Check out the repo
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - run: pip install dbt-postgres==1.7.4
      - run: dbt deps
questions.prompt: If the actions/checkout@v4 step were deleted from this job entirely, what would actually happen when the later steps ran?
options: pip install and dbt deps would still run, but dbt deps would have no retail-orders-analytics project files to install packages for, since the runner starts as an empty machine with no code on it at all
Nothing would change — GitHub automatically clones the repository onto every runner regardless of the workflow's steps
The workflow would fail immediately at the setup-python step specifically
actions/checkout@v4 only matters for private repositories, so this would have no effect on a public one
questions.explain: A runner starts as an empty virtual machine with nothing on it. actions/checkout@v4 is what clones the repository onto it. Without that step, later steps that depend on the project's files — like dbt deps reading dbt_project.yml — have nothing to actually work against.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about why retail-orders-analytics's CI workflow runs dbt build instead of dbt run and dbt test as two separate commands, per Lesson 21.
options: dbt build runs models, tests, seeds, and snapshots together in dependency order
If stg_orders's tests fail, dbt build stops before ever trying to build fct_orders on top of broken data
Running dbt run then dbt test as two separate commands would build every model first regardless of upstream test failures
dbt build and dbt test are two names for the exact same command with no behavioral difference
dbt build skips running tests entirely and only builds models
questions.explain: dbt build runs everything together in dependency order, so a failing test on an upstream model actually stops downstream models from building on top of broken data. Running dbt run and dbt test separately would build every model first, test failures or not — a meaningfully worse default for CI.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: inside profiles.yml, dbt's built-in Jinja function for reading a value from an environment variable at run time — rather than hardcoding it — is ________().
questions.explain: env_var(...) lets profiles.yml pull real connection details (host, user, password) from environment variables at run time instead of writing anything sensitive into the file as literal text.

questions.prompt: Match each condition from retail-orders-analytics's workflow to the moment it's actually designed to match, per Lesson 22.
right: Points dbt at the disposable schema used while a change is still being reviewed
Every proposed change, checked before it's trusted enough to merge
Points dbt at the real production schema once a change is trusted
Only a real push landing directly on main — exactly what a merge produces
questions.explain: The pull_request condition gates the build-and-test job to every proposed change. The push-to-main condition gates the deploy job to exactly what a real merge produces. --target ci points at the disposable review schema, while --target prod points at the real production schema once a change is trusted.

questions.prompt: If this step's run: line were changed to echo "$DB_PASSWORD" for debugging, what would actually show up in the workflow's log?
options: GitHub automatically masks the secret's value as *** in the log output, even though the step itself printed it
The real password, printed in plain text, exactly as a normal environment variable would be
The step fails immediately with a syntax error, since secrets can't be referenced inside env: at all
Nothing — echo is disabled inside any step that references a secret
questions.explain: GitHub automatically masks a secret's value as *** anywhere it shows up in a run's log, even if a step accidentally prints it with something like echo. This is a real, automatic safety net, not something that has to be configured.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about what the capstone brief in Lesson 24 actually requires a finished repository to demonstrate.
options: At least one feature built on its own branch, merged via a real pull request, not a direct push to main
A deliberately broken commit, opened as a PR, showing a real red X — proof the pipeline actually catches something
A deploy job gated to only run on a push to main, using a separate --target from the CI job
Every commit message must be exactly one word long
Real secrets configured in GitHub, referenced via ${{ secrets.* }}, with nothing sensitive committed to the repository
questions.explain: The brief requires a feature merged through a real PR, a deliberately broken commit proving the pipeline catches failures, a separately-gated deploy job with its own target, and real secrets configured on GitHub rather than committed. Nothing in the brief says anything about commit message length.

questions.prompt: Put these in the order Lesson 25 recommends walking a stranger through your capstone repository.
items: Show the .gitignore, proving you know what belongs in version control and what doesn't
Show a real pull request with actual review comments and a suggestion
Read the workflow file out loud, naming its trigger, job, and steps
Show a failed run, then a passing one, proving the pipeline actually catches something real
Explain the deploy job, and why its credentials are scoped differently from CI's
questions.explain: The recommended walkthrough starts with the .gitignore, moves to a real reviewed pull request, then the workflow file itself, then proof via a failed-then-passing run, and finishes with the deploy job and its separately scoped credentials — the exact order Lesson 25 lays out for a credible portfolio presentation.
